entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.1-Prov.6.5">Pro 6:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen10712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10713" type="x-p"/> The author warns against suretyship; or rather, he advises that if one has made himself surety, he should as quickly as possible withdraw from the snare. 1 My son, if thou hast become surety for thy neighbour,    Hast given thy hand for another: 2 Thou art entangled in the words of thy mouth,    Ensnared in the words of thy mouth. 3 Do this then, my son, and free thyself -    For thou hast come under the power of thy neighbour -    Go, instantly entreat and importune thy neighbour. 4 Give no sleep to thine eyes,    And no slumber to thine eyelids; 5 Tear thyself free like a gazelle from his hand,    And as a bird from the hand of the fowler. <div eID="gen10713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10714" type="x-p"/> The chief question here is, whether ל after ערב introduces him for whom or with whom one becomes surety. Elsewhere ערב (R. רב, whence also ארב, <hi type="italic">nectere</hi>, to twist close and compact) with the accusative of the person means to become surety for any one, to represent him as a surety, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.15">Pro 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.16">Pro 20:16</reference> (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.13">Pro 27:13</reference>), <reference osisRef="Gen.43.9">Gen 43:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.44.33">Gen 44:33</reference> (as with the accusative of the matter, to pledge anything, to deposit it as a pledge, <reference osisRef="Jer.30.21">Jer 30:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.5.3">Neh 5:3</reference>, = שׂים, Arab. waḍ'a, <reference osisRef="Job.17.3">Job 17:3</reference>); and to become surety with any one is expressed, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.18">Gen 17:18</reference>, by ערב לפני. The phrase ערב ל is not elsewhere met with, and is thus questionable. If we look to <reference osisRef="Prov.6.3">Pro 6:3</reference>, the רע (רעה) mentioned there cannot possibly be the creditor with whom one has become surety, for so impetuous and urgent an application to him would be both purposeless and unbecoming. But if he is meant for whom one has become surety, then certainly לרעך is also to be understood of the same person, and ל is thus <hi type="italic">dat. commodi</hi>; similar to this is the Targumic ערבוּתא על, suretyship for any one, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.18">Pro 17:18</reference>; Pro 22:26. But is the זר, 1b, distinguished from רעך, the stranger with whom one has become surety? The parallels <reference osisRef="Prov.11.15">Pro 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.16">Pro 20:16</reference>, where זר denotes the person whom one represents, show that in both lines one and the same person is meant; זר is in the Proverbs equivalent to אחר, each different from the person in the discourse, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.17">Pro 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.27.2">Pro 27:2</reference> - thus, like רעך, denotes not the friend, but generally him to whom one stands in any kind of relation, even a very external one, in a word, the fellow-creatures or neighbours, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.28">Pro 24:28</reference> (cf. the Arab. sahbk and ḳarynk, which are used as vaguely and superficially). It is further a question, whether we have to explain 1b: if thou hast given thine hand to another, or for another. Here also we are without evidence from the usage of the language; for the phrase תּקע כּף, or merely תּקע, appears to be used of striking the hand in suretyship where it elsewhere occurs without any further addition, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.18">Pro 17:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.26">Pro 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.11.15">Pro 11:15</reference>; however, <reference osisRef="Job.17.3">Job 17:3</reference>, נתקע ליד appears the same: to strike into the hand of any one, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to give to him the hand-stroke. From this passage Hitzig concludes that the surety gave the hand-stroke, without doubt in the presence of witnesses, first of all of the creditor, to the debtor, as a sign that he stood for him. But this idea is unnatural, and the “without doubt” melts into air. He on whose hand the stroke falls is always the person to whom one gives suretyship, and confirms it by the hand-stroke. Job also, <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>, means to say: who else but Thou, O Lord, could give to me a pledge, viz., of my innocence? If now the זר, v. 1b, is, as we have shown, not the creditor,<note placement="foot">A translation by R. Joseph Joel of Fulda, 1787, whose autograph MS Baer possesses, renders the passage not badly thus: - “My son, if thou hast become surety for thy friend, and hast given the hand to another, then thou art bound by thy word, held by thy promise. Yet do what I say to thee, my son: Be at pains as soon as thou canst to get free, otherwise thou art in the power of thy friend; shun no trouble, be urgent with thy friend.”</note> but the debtor, then is the ל the <hi type="italic">dat. commodi</hi>, as 1a, and the two lines perfectly correspond. תּקע properly means to drive, to strike with a resounding noise, cogn. with the Arab. wak'a, which may be regarded as its intrans. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.6-Prov.6.8">Pro 6:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen10717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10718" type="x-p"/> As Elihu (<reference osisRef="Job.35.11">Job 35:11</reference>) says that God has set the beasts as our teachers, so he sends the sluggard to the school of the ant (<hi type="italic">Ameise</hi>), so named (in Germ.) from its industry (<hi type="italic">Emsigkeit</hi>): 6 Go to the ant, sluggard;    Consider her ways, and be wise! 7 She that hath no judge,    Director, and ruler: 8 She prepareth in summer her food,    Has gathered in harvest her store. <div eID="gen10718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10719" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> written mostly under the לך separates the inseparable. The thought, Go to the ant, sluggard! permits no other distinction than in the vocative; but the <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> of לך אל־נמלה is changed into <hi type="italic">Munach</hi><note placement="foot">Cod. 1294 accentuates לך אל־נמלה; and that, according to Ben-Asher’s rule, is correct.</note> on account of the nature of the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>-word, which consists of only two syllables without the counter-tone. The ant has for its Hebrew-Arabic name נמלה, from the R. נם (Isaiah, p. 687), which is first used of the sound, which expresses the idea of the low, dull, secret - thus of its active and yet unperceived motion; its Aramaic name in the Peshîto, ûmenaa', and in the Targ. שׁוּמשׁמנא (also Arab. sumsum, simsim, of little red ants), designates it after its quick activity, its busy running hither and thither (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Fleischer in Levy’s <hi type="italic">Chald. Wörterb</hi>. ii. 578). She is a model of unwearied and well-planned labour. From the plur. דּרכיה it is to be concluded that the author observed their art in gathering in and laying up in store, carrying burdens, building their houses, and the like (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the passages in the Talmud and Midrash in the Hamburg <hi type="italic">Real-Encyclopädie für Bibel und Talmud</hi>, 1868, p. 83f.). To the ant the sluggard (עצל, Aram. and Arab. עטל, with the fundamental idea of weight and dulness) is sent, to learn from her to be ashamed, and to be taught wisdom.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.9-Prov.6.11">Pro 6:9-11</reference> <div eID="gen10722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10723" type="x-p"/> After the poet has admonished the sluggard to take the ant as an example, he seeks also to rouse him out of his sleepiness and indolence: 9 How long, O sluggard, wilt thou lie?    When wilt thou rise up from thy sleep? 10 “A little sleep, a little slumber,    A little folding of the hands to rest!” 11 So comes like a strong robber thy poverty,    And thy want as an armed man.  <reference osisRef="Prov.6.9-Prov.6.10">Pro 6:9-10</reference> <div eID="gen10723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10724" type="x-p"/> The awakening cry, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.9">Pro 6:9</reference>, is not of the kind that Paul could have it in his mind, Eph 5:14. עצל has, as the vocative, <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> after it, and is, on account of the <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi>, in correct editions accentuated not with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, but <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>. The words, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.10">Pro 6:10</reference>, are not an ironical call (sleep only yet a little while, but in truth a long while), but <hi type="italic">per mimesin</hi> the reply of the sluggard with which he turns away the unwelcome disturber. The plurals with מעט sound like self-delusion: yet a little, but a sufficient! To fold the hands, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to cross them over the breast, or put them into the bosom, denotes also, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.5">Ecc 4:5</reference>, the idler. חבּוּק, <hi type="italic">complicatio</hi> (cf. in Livy, <hi type="italic">compressis quod aiunt manibus sidere</hi>; and Lucan, 2:292, <hi type="italic">compressas tenuisse manus</hi>), for formed like שׁקּוּי, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.8">Pro 3:8</reference>, and the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. שׁכב like חסר, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.21">Pro 10:21</reference>, and שׁפל, Pro 16:19. The <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>. connects itself with the words heard from the mouth of the sluggard, which are as a hypothetical antecedent thereto: if thou so sayest, and always again sayest, then this is the consequence, that suddenly and inevitably poverty and want come upon thee. That מהלּך denotes the <hi type="italic">grassator</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, vagabond (Arab. dawwar, one who wanders much about), or the robber or foe (like the Arab. 'aduww, properly <hi type="italic">transgressor finium</hi>), is not justified by the usage of the language; הלך signifies, <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.4">2Sa 12:4</reference>, the traveller, and מהלּך is one who rides quickly forward, not directly a κακὸς ὁδοιπόρος (lxx).

Pro 6:9-10 The awakening cry, Pro 6:9 , is not of the kind that Paul could have it in his mind, Eph 5:14. עצל has, as the vocative, Pasek after it, and is, on account of the Pasek , in correct editions accentuated not with Munach , but Mercha . The words, Pro 6:10 , are not an ironical call (sleep only yet a little while, but in truth a long while), but per mimesin the reply of the sluggard with which he turns away the unwelcome disturber. The plurals with מעט sound like self-delusion: yet a little, but a sufficient! To fold the hands, i.e. , to cross them over the breast, or put them into the bosom, denotes also, Ecc 4:5 , the idler. חבּוּק, complicatio (cf. in Livy, compressis quod aiunt manibus sidere ; and Lucan, 2:292, compressas tenuisse manus ), for formed like שׁקּוּי, Pro 3:8 , and the inf . שׁכב like חסר, Pro 10:21 , and שׁפל, Pro 16:19. The perf. consec . connects itself with the words heard from the mouth of the sluggard, which are as a hypothetical antecedent thereto: if thou so sayest, and always again sayest, then this is the consequence, that suddenly and inevitably poverty and want come upon thee. That מהלּך denotes the grassator , i.e. , vagabond (Arab. dawwar, one who wanders much about), or the robber or foe (like the Arab. 'aduww, properly transgressor finium ), is not justified by the usage of the language; הלך signifies, 2Sa 12:4 , the traveller, and מהלּך is one who rides quickly forward, not directly a κακὸς ὁδοιπόρος (lxx).

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.12-Prov.6.15">Pro 6:12-15</reference> <div eID="gen10725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10726" type="x-p"/> There follows now a third brief series of instructions, which run to a conclusion with a deterring prospect similar to the foregoing. 12 A worthless man, a wicked man,      Is he who practiseth falsehood with his mouth; 13 Who winketh with his eyes, scrapeth with his foot,      Pointeth with his fingers. 14 Malice is in his heart,      He deviseth evil at all times,      He spreadeth strife. 15 Therefore suddenly his destruction shall come,      Suddenly shall he be destroyed, and there is no remedy. <div eID="gen10726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10727" type="x-p"/> It is a question, what is the subject and what the predicate in Pro 6:12. Thus much is clear, that upon him who is here described according to his deceitful conduct the sentence of condemnation shall fall. He who is so described is thus subject, and אדם בּליּעל is without doubt predicate. But does the complex subject begin with אישׁ און? Thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Hitzig: “A worthless man is the wicked man who....” But the interchange of עדם and אישׁ is a sign of parallel relation; and if 12b belonged attributively to אישׁ און, then since אישׁ האון is not used, it ought at least to have been continued by ההולך. The general moral categories, 12a, are thus predicates, as was indeed besides probable; the copious division of the subject demands also in point of style a more developed predicate. <reference osisRef="Prov.16.27">Pro 16:27</reference> is simpler in plan, and also logically different. There the expression is, as is usual, אישׁ בליעל. Since אדם און is not possible, the author uses instead בליעל. This word, composed of בּלי and יעל (from יעל, ועל, to be useful, to be good for), so fully serves as one word, that it even takes the article, 1Sa 25:25. It denotes worthlessness, generally in a chain of words in the genitive, but also the worthless, <reference osisRef="Job.34.18">Job 34:18</reference>; and it is to be so taken here, for אדם does not form a <hi type="italic">constructivus</hi>, and never governs a genitive. בליעל is thus a virtual adjective (as <hi type="italic">nequam</hi> in <hi type="italic">homo nequam</hi>); the connection is like that of אדם רשׁע, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.7">Pro 11:7</reference>, and elsewhere, although more appositional than this pure attributive. Synonymous with בליעל is און (from <hi type="italic">an</hi>, to breathe), wickedness, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, want of all moral character. Thus worthless and wicked is he who practises deceit with his mouth (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.4.24">Pro 4:24</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, who makes language the means of untruthfulness and uncharitableness. עקּשׁוּת פּה is meant in a moral sense, but without excluding that distortion of the mouth which belongs to the mimicry of the malicious. It is the accus. of the object; for הלך is also bound in a moral sense with the accusative of that which one practises, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, dealing with, exercises himself in, <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pro 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.18">Pro 28:18</reference>, Isa 33:15.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.16-Prov.6.19">Pro 6:16-19</reference> <div eID="gen10730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10731" type="x-p"/> What now follows is not a separate section (Hitzig), but the corroborative continuation of that which precedes. The last word (מדנים, strife) before the threatening of punishment, 14b, is also here the last. The thought that no vice is a greater abomination to God than the (in fact satanical) striving to set men at variance who love one another, clothes itself in the form of the numerical proverb which we have already considered, pp. 12, 13. From that place we transfer the translation of this example of a <hi type="italic">Midda</hi>: - 16 There are six things which Jahve hateth,      And seven are an abhorrence to His soul: 17 Haughty eyes, a lying tongue,      And hands that shed innocent blood; 18 An heart that deviseth the thoughts of evil,      Feet that hastily run to wickedness, 19 One that uttereth lies as a false witness,      And he who soweth strife between brethren. <div eID="gen10731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10732" type="x-p"/> The sense is not, that the six things are hateful to God, and the seventh an abomination to Him besides (Löwenstein); the <hi type="italic">Midda</hi>-form in <reference osisRef="Amos.1.3-Amos.2.6">Amos 1:3-2:6</reference>, and in the proverb in <reference osisRef="Job.5.19">Job 5:19</reference>, shows that the seven are to be numbered separately, and the seventh is the <hi type="italic">non plus ultra</hi> of all that is hated by God. We are not to translate: <hi type="italic">sex haecce odit</hi>, for המּה, הנּה, (הם, הן) points backwards and hitherwards, but not, as אלּה, forwards to that immediately following; in that case the words would be שׁשׁ אלה, or more correctly האלה שׁשׁ. But also Hitzig’s explanation, “These six things (viz., <reference osisRef="Prov.6.12-Prov.6.15">Pro 6:12-15</reference>) Jahve hateth,” is impossible; for (which is also against that <hi type="italic">haecce</hi>) the substantive pronoun המה nuonorp , הנה (ההמה, ההנה) is never, like the Chald. המּון (המּו), employed as an accus. in the sense of אתהם, אתהן, it is always (except where it is the virtual gen. connected with a preposition) only the nom., whether of the subject or of the predicate; and where it is the nom. of the predicate, as <reference osisRef="Deut.20.15">Deu 20:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.19">Isa 51:19</reference>, substantival clauses precede in which הנה (המה) represents the substantive verb, or, more correctly, in which the logical copula resulting from the connection of the clause itself remains unexpressed. Accordingly, 'שׂנא ה is a relative clause, and is therefore so accentuated here, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.30.15">Pro 30:15</reference> and elsewhere: <hi type="italic">sex</hi> (<hi type="italic">sunt</hi>) <hi type="italic">ea quae Deus odit, et septem</hi> (<hi type="italic">sunt</hi>) <hi type="italic">abominatio animae ejus</hi>. Regarding the statement that the soul of God hates anything, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Isa 1:14. תועבות, an error in the writing occasioned by the numeral (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.26.25">Pro 26:25</reference>), is properly corrected by the Kerı̂; the poet had certainly the singular in view, as <reference osisRef="Prov.3.32">Pro 3:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.11.1">Pro 11:1</reference>, when he wrote תועבת. The first three characteristics are related to each other as mental, verbal, actual, denoted by the members of the body by means of which these characteristics come to light. The virtues are taken all together as a body (organism), and meekness is its head. Therefore there stands above all, as the sin of sins, the <hi type="italic">mentis elatae tumor</hi>, which expresses itself in <hi type="italic">elatum</hi> (<hi type="italic">grande</hi>) <hi type="italic">supercilium</hi>: עינים רמות, the feature of the רם, haughty (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.18.28">Psa 18:28</reference> with <reference osisRef="2Sam.22.28">2Sa 22:28</reference>), is the opposite of the feature of the שׁח עינים, <reference osisRef="Job.22.29">Job 22:29</reference>; עין is in the O.T. almost always (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Sol 4:9) fem., and adjectives of course form no dual. The second of these characteristics is the lying tongue, and the third the murderous hands. דּם־נקי is innocent blood as distinguished from דּם הנּקי, the blood of the innocent, Deu 19:13.<note placement="foot">The writing דּם follows the Masoretic rule, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Kimchi, <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 205b, and Heidenheim under <reference osisRef="Deut.19.10">Deu 19:10</reference>, where in printed editions of the text (also in Norzi’s) the irregular form דּם נקי is found. Besides, the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> is to be given to דּם־, so that one may not read it dom, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, שׁשׁ־מאות, <reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Gen 7:11</reference>, that one may not read it שׁשׁ־.</note>

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.23">Pro 6:23</reference> <div eID="gen10742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10743" type="x-p"/> Since in היא the idea of wisdom and of wholesome doctrine lie in one another, the author can proceed with proof: <div eID="gen10743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10744" type="x-p"/> For a lamp is the commandment, and instruction a light (Jerome <hi type="italic">et lex lux</hi>); <div eID="gen10744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10745" type="x-p"/> And a way of life, disciplinary reproofs. <div eID="gen10745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10746" type="x-p"/> That תורה has here not the positive, specifically Israelitish sense, but the generalized sense of instruction in conformity with truth regarding the will of God and the duty of man, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 42. This instruction mediated by man, but of divine origin, is אור, light, which enlightens the man who submits to it; and the commandment, מצוה, which directs men in every case to do what is right, and forbids that which is wrong (including the prohibition <reference osisRef="Lev.4.2">Lev 4:2</reference>), is נר, a lamp which, kindled at that light, enlightens all the darkness of ignorance with reference to human conduct and its consequences. אור and נר are related to each other as general and particular, primary and derivative. Löwenstein accentuates incorrectly תּורהו אור instead of תּורהו אור (as the Cod. 1294 and the 3 Erfurt Codd.); <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on the retrogression of the tone, not existing here, under Pro 3:15. The gen. מוּסר denotes the object or character of the admonition: not disciplinary in the external sense of the word, but rather moral, having in view discipline in the sense of education, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, moral edification and elevation. Such corrections are דּרך חיּים, the way to true life, direction how to obtain it.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.25-Prov.6.26">Pro 6:25-26</reference> <div eID="gen10750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10751" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">proaemium</hi> of these twelve proverbial discourses is now at an end. Wisdom herself begins striking the note of the Decalogue: 25 Long not for her beauty in thy heart,      And let her not catch thee with her eyelids; 26 Because for a harlot one cometh down to a piece of bread,      And a man’s wife lieth in wait for a precious soul. <div eID="gen10751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10752" type="x-p"/> The warning 25a is in the spirit of the “thou shalt not covet,” <reference osisRef="Exod.20.17">Exo 20:17</reference>, and the ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὑτοῦ, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28">Mat 5:28</reference>, of the Preacher on the Mount. The Talmudic proverb הרהודי עבירה קשו מעבירה (<hi type="italic">Joma</hi> 29a) means only that the imagination of the sinful act exhausts the body even more than the act itself. The warning, “let her not catch thee with her eyelids,” refers to her (the adulteress’s) coquettish ogling and amorous winking. In the reason added, beginning with כּי בעד־ (thus it is to be punctuated), there is the appositional connection אשּׁה זונה, Gesen. §113; the idea of זונה goes over into 26b. “לחם כּכּר [ = כּרכּר, R. kr, to round, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Gen 49:5], properly a circle of bread, is a small round piece of bread, such as is still baked in Italy (<hi type="italic">pagnotta</hi>) and in the East (Arab. ḳurṣ), here an expression for the smallest piece” (Fl.). בּעד (<hi type="italic">constr</hi>. of בּעד), as <reference osisRef="Job.2.4">Job 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.14">Isa 32:14</reference>, is used in the sense of ὑπέρ, <hi type="italic">pro</hi>, and with עד there is connected the idea of the coming down to this low point. Ewald, Bertheau explain after the lxx, τιμὴ γὰρ πόρνης ὅση καὶ ἑνὸς ἄρτου, γυνὴ δὲ ἀνδρῶν τιμίας ψυχὰς ἀγρεύει. But nothing is said here of price (reward); the parallelism is synonymous, not antithetic: he is doubly threatened with loss who enters upon such a course. The adulterer squanders his means (<reference osisRef="Prov.29.3">Pro 29:3</reference>) to impoverishment (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the mention of a loaf of bread in the description of poverty <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.36">1Sa 2:36</reference>), and a man’s wife (but at the same time seeking converse with another) makes a prey of a precious soul; for whoever consents to adulterous converse with her, loses not perhaps his means, but certainly freedom, purity, dignity of soul, yea, his own person. צוּד comprehends - as צידון, fisher’s town [Zidon], Arab. ṣyâd, hunter and fisher, show - all kinds of hunting, but in Hebr. is used only of the hunting of wild beasts. The root-meaning (cf. צדיּה) is to spy, to seize.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.30-Prov.6.31">Pro 6:30-31</reference> <div eID="gen10756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10757" type="x-p"/> The thief and the adulterer are now placed in comparison with one another, in such a way that adultery is supposed to be a yet greater crime. 30 One does not treat the thief scornfully if he steals      To satisfy his craving when he is hungry; 31 Being seized, he may restore sevenfold,      Give up the whole wealth of his house. <div eID="gen10757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10758" type="x-p"/> For the most part 30a is explained: even when this is the case, one does not pass it over in the thief as a bagatelle. Ewald remarks: בּוּז ל stands here in its nearest signification of overlooking, whence first follows that of contemning. But this “nearest” signification is devised wholly in favour of this passage; - the interpretation, “they do not thus let the thief pass,” is set aside by Sol 8:1, Sol 8:7; for by 31b, cf. Sol 8:7, and 34a, cf. Sol 8:6, it is proved that from <reference osisRef="Prov.6.30">Pro 6:30</reference> on, reminiscences from the Canticles, which belong to the literature of the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi>, find their way into the Mashal language of the author. Hitzig’s correct supposition, that בּוּז ל always signifies positive contemning, does not necessitate the interrogative interpretation: “Does not one despise the thief if...?” Thus to be understood, the author ought to have written אף כי or גם כי. Michaelis rightly: <hi type="italic">furtum licet merito pro infami in republica habetur, tamen si cum adulterio comparatur, minus probrosum est</hi>. Regarding נפשׁ in the sense of appetite, and even throat and stomach, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Psychologie</hi>, p. 204. A second is, that the thief, if he is seized (but we regard ונמצא not as the <hi type="italic">hypoth. perf</hi>., but as the <hi type="italic">part. deprehensus</hi>), may make compensation for this crime. The fut. ישׁלּם thus to be understood as the potential lies near from this, that a sevenfold compensation of the thing stolen is unheard of in the Israelitish law; it knows only of a twofold, fourfold, fivefold restoration, Ex. 21:37; <reference osisRef="Exod.22.1-Exod.22.3">Exo 22:1-3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.8">Exo 22:8</reference> (cf. Saalschütz, <hi type="italic">Mos. Recht</hi>, p. 554ff.). This excess over that which the law rendered necessary leads into the region of free-will: he (the thief, by which we are now only to think of him whom bitter necessity has made such) may make compensation sevenfold, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, superabundantly; he may give up the whole possessions (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on הון at <reference osisRef="Prov.1.13">Pro 1:13</reference>) of his house, so as not merely to satisfy the law, but to appease him against whom he has done wrong, and again to gain for himself an honoured name. What is said in <reference osisRef="Prov.6.30">Pro 6:30</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.6.31">Pro 6:31</reference> is perfectly just. One does not contemn a man who is a thief through poverty, he is pitied; while the adulterer goes to ruin under all circumstances of contempt and scorn. And: theft may be made good, and that abundantly; but adultery and its consequences are irreparable.

Regarding being mad (<hi type="italic">herzlos</hi> = <hi type="italic">heartless</hi>) = <hi type="italic">amens</hi> (<hi type="italic">excors, vecors</hi>), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Psychologie</hi>, p. 254. משׁחית נפשׁו is he who goes to ruin with wilful perversity. It is the worst and most inextinguishable dishonouring of oneself. Singularly Behaji: who annihilates it (his soul), with reference to Deu 21:12. Eccl. 4:17, where עשׂה would be equivalent to בּטּל, καταργεῖν, which is untrue and impossible.<note placement="foot">Behaji ought rather to have referred to Zep 3:19; <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.27">Eze 7:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.14">Eze 22:14</reference>; but there עשׂה את means <hi type="italic">agere cum aliquo</hi>, as we say: <hi type="italic">mit jemandem abrechnen</hi> (to settle accounts with any one).</note> נגע refers to the corporal punishment inflicted on the adulterer by the husband (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.8">Deu 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.21.5">Deu 21:5</reference>); Hitzig, who rejects <reference osisRef="Prov.6.32">Pro 6:32</reference>, refers it to the stripes which were given to the thief according to the law, but these would be called מכּה (מכּות). entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Prov.6.34-Prov.6.35">Pro 6:34-35</reference> <div eID="gen10759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10760" type="x-p"/> One who has been stolen from is to be appeased, but not the injured husband. 34 For jealousy is the fury of a husband,      And he spareth not in the day of vengeance. 35 He regardeth not any ransom,      And is not contented though thou offerest to him gifts ever so great. <div eID="gen10760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10761" type="x-p"/> The connection marks קנאה as the subject; for it respects carnal intercourse with another’s wife. Jealousy is not usually חמה, the glow of anger (from יחם, as שׁנה from ישׁן), but חמת־גּבר (constr. as שׂנת), the glow of a man’s anger, who with the putting forth of all his manly strength will seek satisfaction to his wounded honour. גּבר, here significant for אישׁ, with the fundamental idea of strength, firmness; cf. Arab. jabr, to make fast, to put right again something broken in pieces, particularly a broken vessel, hence <hi type="italic">Algebra</hi>, properly the operation by which an incomplete magnitude is completed (Fl.). The following ולא־יחמּל (with the orthophonic <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Prov.6.25">Pro 6:25</reference> יחמּד, and with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>) is connected with גבר, with definite reference to the man whom the faithless guest has made a cuckold. When the day comes in which the adultery brought to light demands and admits of vengeance, then, wounded in his right and in his honour, he knows no mercy; he pays no regard to any atonement or recompense by which the adulterer seeks to appease him and induce him not to inflict the punishment that is due: he does not consent, even though thou makest ever so great the gift whereby thou thinkest to gain him. The phrase נשׂא פנים, πρόσωπον λαμβάνειν, signifies elsewhere to receive the countenance, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the appearance and the impression of a man, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to let it impress one favourably; here it is used of the כּפר, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the means by which covering, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, non-punishment, pardon of the crime, impunity of the guilty, is obtained. Regarding אבה, to consent to, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 1:10. שׂחד, Aram. שׂוּחד, is a gift, particularly bribery. That the language may again finally assume the form of an address, it beautifully rounds itself off.  <chapter eID="Prov.6"/> <div eID="gen10761" type="x-p"/>
